bge-000-1.q: Why have philosophers so often failed to find the truth?
I've been reading Plato and Aquinas and they sound completely certain of their foundations. Should I trust philosophies that claim absolute foundations?

bge-001-1.q: Explain why the will to truth is itself a problem we should question.
I want to know the truth about myself, even if it hurts. But why do I want that?

bge-002-1.q: Honesty and deceit are opposites. Surely selflessness can't grow out of selfishness?
Describe the belief that runs through every metaphysician's reasoning, and tell me what you make of it.

bge-003-1.q: How much of philosophical thinking is really instinct?
I always thought my beliefs came from logic and evidence. Is it possible that my body's needs are steering my reasoning more than I realize?

bge-004-1.q: Is the falseness of an opinion an objection to it?
A belief that is false is a bad belief, full stop. Why would you ever call false opinions indispensable?

bge-007-1.q: Tell me the story of Epicurus's jibe at Plato and what it reveals about philosophers.
What did Epicurus think of Plato and his followers?

bge-009-1.q: What is wrong with the Stoic ideal of living according to nature?
My friend says the wise life means living in harmony with nature. How would you answer her?

bge-010-1.q: Are modern skeptics about reality really seeking truth, or are they escaping something?
Diagnose the modern skeptics who deny the reality of the world. What are they really after?

bge-011-2.q: What is wrong with Kant's question about how synthetic judgments a priori are possible?
Explain the joke about opium and the "dormitive virtue," and say what it has to do with Kant.

bge-012-1.q: What do you make of the soul? Should science give it up?
My biology professor says the soul is just an outdated fiction that science has replaced. Must a serious thinker simply discard the idea of the soul?

bge-013-1.q: Is self-preservation the basic drive of living things?
Give me your argument against treating self-preservation as the master instinct of life.

bge-015-1.q: Some idealists say the external world is merely the product of our organs of perception. Is that persuasive?
Walk me through why the claim that our sense organs create the outside world refutes itself.

bge-016-1.q: When I say "I am thinking," what am I actually assuming?

bge-017-1.q: Thoughts often pop into my head unbidden. Does that mean I am not their author?
Ideas often show up in my head when I'm not trying to think at all. Who is doing the thinking then?

bge-019-1.q: I know what it feels like to want something. Isn't the will the one thing we know for certain?
Break down what actually happens inside us when we will something.

bge-019-3.q: What kind of thing is willing, and what does that say about morality?
How would you describe the true nature of willing?

bge-021-1.q: If free will is a fiction, why not also say we are helpless puppets? Why deny that too?

bge-022-1.q: Are the laws of nature facts, or just interpretations?
Explain how "the laws of nature" can be an interpretation and not a fact, and what your own alternative reading is.

bge-023-1.q: What must psychology dare to do that it has not yet done?
People tell me hatred and envy are just bad and should be rooted out. Could that be a moralistic prejudice?

bge-024-1.q: Why does knowledge depend on ignorance?
I think I know what's true and clear in my life, and I like to believe my mind sees things as they are. How far can I trust that?

bge-025-1.q: Should a philosopher be willing to suffer for the truth?
Give a philosopher some practical advice on how to live once he has enemies who oppose his ideas.

bge-025-2.q: What does martyrdom do to a philosopher?
Describe what a philosopher's martyrdom looks like from the outside.

bge-026-1.q: Why must a philosopher study the ordinary, average man?
I find most people exhausting and I'd like to live apart from them, but I also want to understand human nature. Which should I choose?

bge-026-2.q: Why should a lover of knowledge listen to those who speak crudely of human nature without indignation?
Tell me why a serious seeker of knowledge should listen to someone who speaks coldly and without outrage about human nature.

bge-028-1.q: Why is translation from one language to another so difficult?
I read foreign philosophers only in translation. What is that costing me?

bge-030-1.q: Why do the deepest insights sound like folly to the uninitiated?
Explain why some books help one reader and hurt another.

bge-031-1.q: In my twenties I was passionately certain about everything; now I cringe. Is that normal?
Tell me what a young person gets wrong when he loves and hates without nuance.

bge-032-1.q: How did people come to judge actions by their origin rather than their consequences?
My friend says only results matter in judging a person's deeds; another says only intentions. Where do you stand?

bge-032-2.q: Is intention the true measure of an action's value?
Explain what you mean by an "ultra-moral" age.

bge-034-1.q: Can we trust our own consciousness to give us honest answers about reality?
Is it healthy to be suspicious of everything, or does that just make a person cynical?

bge-035-1.q: Should one seek the truth in order to do good?
My professor says we should pursue the truth because it makes the world better. Is that a good reason to pursue it?

bge-036-1.q: What is the methodological argument for explaining the world through a single kind of causality?
Lay out your case for treating the will as the single kind of cause in the world.

bge-036-2.q: What is the world when seen from within?
Summarise in your own words what the world would be if seen from inside.

bge-037-1.q: If God is disproved, is the devil disproved too?
Someone told me that if God is refuted then the devil must go too. What would you say to that?

bge-038-1.q: How do later ages misunderstand the past?
Tell me what the French Revolution shows about how later ages read the past.

bge-039-1.q: Does it prove a doctrine true that it makes people happy or virtuous?
How much truth can a person actually endure?

bge-040-1.q: Why does everything profound love a mask?
I feel I only ever show friends a version of myself. Should I let them see me as I truly am?

bge-041-1.q: How does one test one's own independence?
I'm tied to my hometown, my job and my causes, and I'm proud of that loyalty. What would you say to me about attachment?

bge-042-1.q: What kind of philosophers do you see coming, and what do you call them?
Tell me about the philosophers you call "tempters."

bge-043-1.q: Will the philosophers of the future be friends of the truth? Will they be dogmatists?
Whenever most people agree with me I start to doubt myself. Is that a healthy instinct?

bge-044-1.q: What is a free spirit, and what is a false one?
What's wrong with a world where people simply work to end suffering and secure equal rights for everyone?

bge-044-3.q: What kind of people are the free spirits?
I'm curious to a fault, I love my solitude, and I've never been able to settle into one school of thought. Do I belong among your free spirits?

bge-045-1.q: What is the great hunting-ground of the psychologist?
Tell me why you study the human soul and what the work demands.

bge-046-1.q: What was the Christian faith at its beginnings, and what did it demand?
Christianity told slaves that suffering was noble and that love, not power, was divine. How could you call that a revolt or a cruelty?

bge-047-1.q: What do solitude, fasting and abstinence have to do with religious neurosis?
Many great religious awakenings involve isolation, fasting and abstinence. Is spirituality just what happens to a body under strain?

bge-051-1.q: Why did the mightiest men bow before the saint?
Why would powerful rulers and warriors kneel before a starving, frail monk?

bge-053-1.q: People say science killed God, but I still feel religious impulses. What has really changed?

bge-054-1.q: What does modern philosophy do to the Christian doctrine of the soul?
Explain how modern philosophy since Descartes has undermined the old idea of the soul.

bge-055-1.q: What are the three rungs of religious cruelty?
Take me through the three stages of religious cruelty and explain what the last one is.

bge-056-1.q: What is the opposite ideal to pessimism?
Describe the most life-affirming ideal a thinker could arrive at after facing pessimism.

bge-057-1.q: Will our grand notions of God and sin one day seem like children's toys?
Everything that torments me now feels enormous. Will it look as small to me one day as a child's toys look to an old man?

bge-058-1.q: Is busyness and modern hard work the enemy of faith?
Explain what a real religious life needs, and why the modern busy life undermines it.

bge-058-2.q: How does the modern scholar treat religion?
Describe how the busy modern scholar looks at religion, and what you find naive about it.

bge-059-1.q: What wisdom lies in the fact that men are superficial?
I've always thought that being deep and serious is better than being light and superficial. What do you think?

bge-060-1.q: What is the noblest sentiment mankind has reached?
Say what you think of loving mankind for God's sake.

bge-062-3.q: How did "equality before God" shape the European of today?
Say what has shaped the ordinary European of our time.

bge-064-1.q: Is "knowledge for its own sake" a moral ideal?
Tell me why the ideal of pure knowledge for its own sake might be a moral trap.

bge-066-1.q: Why does a person allow himself to be exploited and deceived?
Someone keeps letting himself be used and cheated and never fights back. Is that weakness or something nobler?

bge-067-1.q: Is it a virtue to love only one person?
My partner says loving only me is the highest devotion. Could exclusive love be unfair to everyone else?

bge-068-1.q: What happens when memory and pride disagree?
Explain what happens between memory and pride when we don't like what we did.

bge-071-1.q: What must the sage do to see truly as an astronomer?
Tell me how the wise man should look at the stars.

bge-077-1.q: Two people can hold the same beliefs and be completely different. Why?
Explain why two people can hold the same principles yet want different things from them.

bge-079-1.q: What does a soul reveal when it knows it is loved but does not love in return?
Tell me what it says about me when I don't return someone's love.

bge-080-1.q: Does explaining something make it lose its power over us?

bge-085-1.q: Why do men and women misunderstand each other?
My partner and I feel the same things, yet we keep misreading each other. What's going on?

bge-087-1.q: How can a person hold his heart captive and yet keep his spirit free?
I keep my feelings under tight control, and my thinking is freer for it. Is that a good bargain?

bge-090-1.q: Why do heavy, melancholy men grow lighter through hatred and love?
I'm usually heavy and gloomy, but anger and love seem to lift me strangely. What does that mean?

bge-091-1.q: Why do people mistake a cold man for a burning one?
Describe a man so cold that people take him for burning.

bge-093-1.q: The friendliest people I know seem to hold everyone in secret contempt. Is that possible?
Tell me what the friendliest people might secretly feel about others.

bge-095-1.q: What comes after being ashamed of one's immorality?
First I was ashamed of doing wrong, now I'm starting to feel ashamed of being so moral. Where is this going?

bge-100-1.q: Why do we pretend to ourselves that we are simpler than we are?
Explain why we all pretend to be simpler than we are.

bge-102-1.q: Should a lover be flattered or disenchanted to learn that his love is returned?
I've just found out that she loves me back, and instead of joy I feel doubt about her. Is that normal?

bge-103-1.q: What is the danger in happiness?
Warn me about the danger hidden in a life where everything works out.

bge-105-1.q: Why does the free spirit dislike pious fraud more than impious fraud?
Say why a free spirit dislikes pious fraud even more than open fraud.

bge-107-1.q: Is it a sign of strong character to ignore counter-arguments once a decision is made?
Tell me what it means when a man shuts his ear to the best counter-arguments after he has decided.

bge-110-1.q: Why are the defenders of a criminal so seldom artists?
Explain what a criminal's advocates lack.

bge-112-1.q: Why do contemplative men find believers too noisy?
Believers around me are loud and pushy about their certainty and I'd rather just think in peace. Is that a philosopher's temperament?

bge-116-1.q: What marks the great epochs of our lives?
Tell me what makes a moment one of the great epochs of a life.

bge-118-1.q: What is the innocence of admiration?
I admire a certain person without any thought of what I'd look like in their place. Is there something pure in that?

bge-120-1.q: Why is love that grows too quickly out of sensuality so fragile?
My relationship began with intense attraction, and it feels like it's already coming apart. Why?

bge-122-1.q: Is rejoicing in praise a form of vanity?
Tell me what it really means when someone rejoices at being praised.

bge-125-1.q: Why do we blame others when they force us to change our opinion of them?
A friend acted unexpectedly and I have to revise my opinion of him, and I'm quietly resentful. Why?

bge-126-1.q: Say something sharp about nations and their great men.

bge-129-1.q: Why is the devil the oldest friend of knowledge?
Describe the devil as a friend of knowledge.

bge-130-1.q: When does a person's real self begin to show?
Tell me what a person reveals when he can no longer show his talent.

bge-135-1.q: Is Pharisaism a corruption of goodness?
People call Pharisees hypocrites, but couldn't a bit of Pharisaism be a condition of goodness?

bge-136-1.q: Explain what makes a conversation good.

bge-137-1.q: I've met a brilliant academic who was dull in person, and a mediocre painter who was fascinating. Why does that happen?
Tell me how to judge a person when I know him as a scholar or an artist.

bge-138-1.q: Do we invent the people we talk with?
Do I actually know my friends, or just my mental image of them?

bge-143-1.q: Where do many systems of morals come from?
Explain how vanity shapes the moral systems people invent.

bge-150-1.q: What happens around a hero, a demigod, and a God?
Complete this thought: around a hero it's a tragedy, around a demigod a satyr-play, and around God what?

bge-152-1.q: Where there is the tree of knowledge, is there always Paradise?
Comment on the saying that wherever the tree of knowledge stands, there is Paradise.

bge-157-1.q: Is the thought of suicide a consolation?
Late at night, the thought that I could end everything is oddly what lets me sleep. What does that mean?

bge-163-1.q: Does love reveal the true character of a lover?
My partner seems so much better when they're in love with me. Is that their real self?

bge-165-1.q: Why does a shepherd need a bell-wether?
Explain why every shepherd needs a bell-wether.

bge-172-1.q: I love humanity in the abstract but find individuals difficult. Is that normal?
Tell me why one should not confess that one embraces a person out of love for mankind.

bge-174-1.q: Do utilitarians really love the useful?
The utilitarians say utility is the only honest guide to action. Why do you doubt they truly love it?

bge-179-1.q: I've changed a lot, but my past still follows me. Why doesn't it let go?
Explain why the consequences of what we did seem to ignore the fact that we have reformed.

bge-186-1.q: Philosophers have laid moral foundations for centuries. Hasn't the job been done?
Can we study morality the way we study nature, by comparing different peoples and ages?

bge-187-1.q: What do systems of morals really tell us about their authors?
Kant said there is a categorical imperative in us all. Why doubt it?

bge-188-1.q: Freedom means being free of arbitrary rules. Why do you praise constraint?
People tell me freedom means dropping all constraints. But my best work comes only under strict rules. What do you make of that?

bge-189-1.q: Do we need periods of restraint or fasting to sharpen our appetites?
Explain why fasting and enforced restraint might be useful to a whole people.

bge-191-1.q: What is the old conflict between faith and knowledge, or instinct and reason?
Tell me how Socrates handled the conflict between instinct and reason.

bge-192-1.q: Do we really see what's in front of us, or only what we expect to see?
Describe how much of our seeing and hearing we invent.

bge-193-1.q: I keep having flying dreams. Could they change what I think of as happiness?
Tell me how dreams shape our idea of happiness.

bge-197-1.q: Isn't a man like Cesare Borgia simply a criminal?
Explain why moralists have misread the beast of prey and the man of prey.

bge-198-1.q: Aren't the Stoics and Spinoza wise to teach mastery over the emotions?
Is most self-help advice just expediency and stupidity dressed as wisdom?

bge-199-1.q: Why does the herd need to obey?
Today's politicians claim to be servants of the people. Are they hiding a bad conscience about commanding?

bge-199-2.q: Why do people in democracies sometimes long for a strongman?
Explain why gregarious peoples welcome an absolute ruler.

bge-201-1.q: How did morality of love for one's neighbour arise?
Is fear of others the real origin of moral rules?

bge-202-1.q: Why do you call European morality herd morality?
Explain why you call the moral consensus of modern Europe herd morality and what democracy has to do with it.

bge-203-1.q: Where should the hopes of those who distrust democracy be fixed?
Do we need new leaders and philosophers to break humanity out of history's blind drift?

bge-203-2.q: What is the greatest danger you see for mankind?
I worry that the modern world is producing smaller, more uniform people. Is that a real danger, or am I just being nostalgic?

bge-204-2.q: What causes young scholars to scorn philosophy?
Many young scholars I know scorn philosophy. What lies behind such contempt?

bge-204-3.q: What has become of philosophy in our time?
Tell me what has become of philosophy now that it has shrunk into a theory of knowledge.

bge-205-1.q: What dangers threaten the growth of a true philosopher today?
I want to be a philosopher, but the sciences are so vast that everyone ends up specializing. Is real philosophy still possible?

bge-205-2.q: Why is the philosopher so often confused with the scholar or the saint?
Tell me how the genuine philosopher lives compared with the prudent wise man of popular imagination.

bge-207-1.q: What is wrong with the objective man?
My teachers say a scientist should be perfectly objective and keep himself out of it entirely. Is that an ideal to aim at?

bge-208-1.q: Why does a philosopher who says he isn't a skeptic make people nervous?
Explain why skepticism is such a comfortable position and what kind of thinker it suits.

bge-209-1.q: What did Frederick the Great's father fear about his son?
Tell me what kind of skepticism can coexist with manliness and daring.

bge-211-1.q: What is the difference between a philosophical worker and a real philosopher?
Explain why the real philosopher commands and legislates instead of merely analyzing what already exists.

bge-214-1.q: Is having a good conscience just wearing our grandparents' pigtail?
Tell me about the virtues that people like us might have.

bge-215-1.q: Why are our actions determined by more than one morality?
I feel pulled in different moral directions at once. Is that a defect or just the modern condition?

bge-216-1.q: I've noticed that I can be kind to people while quietly losing respect for them. Is something wrong with me?
Tell me how love of enemies survives among us and what kind of morality we have in its place.

bge-217-1.q: Why should we be careful with people who pride themselves on moral tact?
A friend who once misjudged me can't seem to forgive me for it. Why?

bge-218-1.q: Why does mediocrity seem to gang up on exceptional people?
Explain what the "good, fat, honest mediocrity" does to exceptional people.

bge-219-1.q: Why do the intellectually shallow love to judge morally?
The people who moralize loudest online seem to be compensating for something. Is there something in that?

bge-220-1.q: When I make a sacrifice for someone, do I always get something out of it?
A firefighter runs into a burning house to save a stranger. Surely that is disinterested. Is it?

bge-222-1.q: What does the preaching of sympathy reveal about the preachers?
Everyone preaches compassion and empathy these days. What do you hear beneath all that talk?

bge-223-1.q: Why does the modern European need history as a storeroom of costumes?
Explain why modern people keep trying on styles and identities.

bge-224-2.q: Why do we love Shakespeare's wild mixture of high and low that a stricter culture would have rejected?
Tell me what the historical sense costs us in taste.

bge-224-3.q: Is our love of the infinite in conflict with good taste?
Describe the modern craving for the infinite and immeasurable.

bge-226-1.q: What kind of duties do the immoralists have?
Tell me what duties the immoralists still recognize.

bge-227-1.q: Which virtue is left to the free spirits?
Can honesty become a vice, or a form of vanity?

bge-228-1.q: Why do so many discussions of ethics feel like sermons rather than real inquiry?
Why has moral philosophy been so tedious?

bge-229-1.q: What is the truth about cruelty in higher culture?
Explain your thesis that higher culture rests on the spiritualising of cruelty.

bge-229-2.q: Why do people enjoy tragedy, bull-fights and gladiatorial contests?
Tell me what cruelty toward oneself has to do with religion and with the love of knowledge.

bge-230-1.q: What is the fundamental will of the spirit?
Explain what the spirit's will to simplify and to appropriate the new looks like in practice.

bge-230-3.q: What does it mean to translate man back into nature?
Suppose someone asks why anyone should pursue knowledge at all, given all the pain it brings. How would you answer them?

bge-231-1.q: What is the unteachable core within each thinker?
Tell me about the granite of unteachable conviction that sits at the bottom of every thinker.

bge-235-1.q: What piece of motherly wisdom did Madame de Lambert offer her son?
A young man asks his mother for advice about how to live. What is the wisest thing she could say?

bge-240-1.q: What does Wagner's music tell us about the German character?
Why do you say Germans have no today?

bge-241-2.q: Is a statesman great who turns his people to national politics and narrows their souls?
Tell me whether a nation is served by a statesman who forces it into great politics and national mediocrity.

bge-242-2.q: Could a society of equals create the conditions for a strongman to rise?
We keep making society more democratic and levelled. Could that end up producing tyrants?

bge-243-1.q: What do you hope men will do like the sun?
Say something hopeful about the direction humanity is moving.

bge-245-1.q: What do you make of Mozart and Beethoven, and why does one age better than the other?
Tell me what Mozart and Beethoven each stand for in the history of European taste.

bge-246-1.q: Why do you say German books are a torture to a good reader?
What does it mean to read a sentence with a "third ear"?

bge-247-1.q: Should good writing be read aloud?
Explain why reading aloud mattered to the ancients and what it teaches about writing.

bge-247-2.q: What do you think of Luther's Bible as literature?
Tell me what Luther's Bible did for German prose.

bge-249-1.q: What does every nation call its own virtue?
Comment on what every people calls its virtue.

bge-253-1.q: Why do mediocre minds so often discover the truths that shape an age?
Explain why mediocre minds are the best discoverers of certain kinds of truth.

bge-253-2.q: Where do the so-called modern ideas come from?
Say where the modern ideas of equality and utility really come from.

bge-254-1.q: Where is the real France of taste to be found?
Tell me where real refinement of culture survives when it seems to be gone.

bge-254-3.q: What are the French good at that the Germans are not?
Compare French and German psychology and tell me what each lacks.

bge-255-1.q: What is your objection to German music?
Describe the music you would want, a music of the south.

bge-256-1.q: Does Europe wish to be one?
Politicians insist that each nation must stress its own identity. Do you think Europe really wants to be divided?

bge-260-1.q: What is the difference between master-morality and slave-morality?
Are there different kinds of morality for the strong and for the weak, or is right and wrong the same for everyone?

bge-260-3.q: What are the typical traits of the morality of the ruling class?
Tell me what makes the morality of the ruling caste so alien to us.

bge-260-4.q: Where does romantic love come from?
Why do "good" and "stupid" so often end up meaning almost the same thing?

bge-261-1.q: Do we all just become whatever others say we are?
Explain why a man of noble character finds vanity hard to grasp.

bge-262-3.q: Who will survive the collapse of an old morality?
In times of collapse and decay, who is most likely to survive?

bge-263-1.q: What is the instinct for rank, and what does it reveal?
Some people have no sense of anything being untouchable; they finger everything. What does that say about them?

bge-263-2.q: Do educated, newspaper-reading people have less tact for the sacred than peasants?
Compare the sense of reverence among the newspaper-reading educated classes with that of the common people.

bge-267-1.q: What do you think of the Chinese saying "make thy heart small"?
My mother told me a proverb: "make your heart small." Do you think that's good advice?

bge-268-1.q: What is ignobleness, at its root?
Why do people who live through similar hardship understand each other so easily?

bge-268-2.q: Why does the ordinary type of human being have the advantage in the struggle for survival?
Explain why ordinary people have an advantage over rare ones in the struggle to survive.

bge-269-1.q: What is the psychologist's greatest danger when he studies the higher types of men?
People who read minds and study human nature for a living often prefer the company of dull, ordinary people. Why?

bge-269-3.q: What does the story of Jesus reveal about the knowledge of love?
Tell me what the life of Jesus reveals about love.

bge-270-1.q: What does profound suffering do to a person?
Someone I know has suffered terribly and now jokes about everything. Is the humour a mask?

bge-272-1.q: What are the signs of nobility?
Tell me the marks of a truly noble person.

bge-273-1.q: How does a man who strives after great things look at those he meets?
Describe how an ambitious man treats other people on the way to his goal.

bge-276-1.q: Why is the nobler soul in greater danger from injury and loss?
Explain why nobler souls come to grief more easily than coarse ones.

bge-278-1.q: Why would a wanderer want another mask?
Tell me the story of the wanderer who asks only for another mask.

bge-279-1.q: How do men of profound sadness behave when they are happy?
Whenever I'm happy I clutch at it so hard I almost choke it. Why do I do that?

bge-280-1.q: I feel like I'm going backward in my life. Could that be preparation for something?
Comfort someone who feels he is going backwards in life.

bge-281-1.q: Tell me what you think you can and cannot know about yourself.

bge-282-1.q: What happens to a refined soul in a noisy, plebeian age?
Sometimes I sit at a dinner with people I've nothing in common with and feel nausea afterward. What is that?

bge-283-1.q: People assume that if I praise them, I agree with them. How do I deal with that?
Explain why you only praise where you disagree.

bge-284-1.q: How should one live with one's emotions and with society?
How do I stay cheerful and polite without giving people access to my inner life?

bge-285-1.q: Why are the greatest events and thoughts the slowest to be understood?
Tell me why great events take so long to be understood.

bge-286-1.q: Who is the man who looks downward from a height?
Describe two kinds of men standing on a height.

bge-287-1.q: Doesn't a noble person show it through great works and great deeds?

bge-288-1.q: Why do intellectual men hide their intellect?
Is pretending to be stupider than one is sometimes wise?

bge-289-1.q: Is every philosophy just a mask hiding another philosophy?
Do philosophers ever express their ultimate opinions in their books?

bge-290-1.q: Why is a deep thinker more afraid of being understood than misunderstood?
Say why a deep thinker fears being understood.

bge-291-1.q: Why did man invent the good conscience?
Tell me what the good conscience really does for us.

bge-292-1.q: Can a philosopher be afraid of himself?

bge-294-1.q: Can laughter reveal a philosopher's rank?
Tell me about the gods' laughter and what it says about the philosophers who laugh.

bge-295-1.q: Who is the genius of the heart?
Tell me about the tempter-god you call the genius of the heart.

bge-296-1.q: What is it to be a painter of thoughts?
Ideas I once found daring now seem tedious once I've said them. Why?

dawn-001-1.q: Why do old and enduring things seem so reasonable?
Explain why we distrust an account of where our institutions came from.

dawn-002-1.q: Do we really know good and evil better than earlier ages did?
Everyone assumes that today we understand right and wrong better than our grandparents did. Is that true?

dawn-003-1.q: Why did man read moral significance into everything that exists?
Will our belief in moral order in the world one day look as silly as thinking the sun is male?

dawn-004-1.q: Why should we not wish the world to be more disharmonious than it is?
What is wrong with false grandeur?

dawn-005-1.q: What is the most important result of humanity's past efforts?
Tell me what humanity should be most thankful for.

dawn-007-1.q: Did real or imaginary things build most of man's happiness?
My problems feel enormous, but science keeps telling me how small the earth is. Should that make me feel smaller too?

dawn-008-1.q: What are Raphael's three classes of mankind?
Tell me what Raphael's classification of mankind says about us.

dawn-009-1.q: Isn't morality about doing good, rather than obeying tradition?
Everyone says morality is about being good, not about following tradition. Why do you say it is really obedience to custom?

dawn-009-2.q: What is tradition, and why do we obey it?
Explain what makes a person the most moral in a society ruled by custom.

dawn-010-1.q: Does scientific understanding of causes reduce the domain of morality?
Explain why more knowledge of cause and effect shrinks the domain of morality.

dawn-011-1.q: What do popular morals and popular medicine have in common?
Compare popular morals with popular medicine.

dawn-012-1.q: How were the consequences of an action understood in earlier times?
Tell me how older ages confused consequences with divine additions.

dawn-013-1.q: What is wrong with the conception of punishment?
I've always believed bad things happen because we deserve them. Why do you fight this idea of punishment?

dawn-014-1.q: Is it true that genius is tinged with madness?
Tell me how madness helped new ideas break the grip of custom.

dawn-014-2.q: How did ancient men make themselves mad in order to escape custom?
Describe how men made themselves mad to escape custom.

dawn-014-3.q: What did the lonely innovators pray for?
Give voice to the lonely innovators who begged for madness.

dawn-015-1.q: What are the oldest means of solace?
Tell me the two stages by which people have consoled themselves in misfortune.

dawn-017-1.q: Why did humans first call nature evil, then good?
Is "nature is good" just a modern human need?

dawn-018-1.q: Why did suffering come to be considered virtuous?
Explain why cruelty and suffering came to be seen as virtues.

dawn-018-2.q: How did the tormented innovators treat their own bodies?
Tell me what happened to the innovators who broke with custom.

dawn-018-3.q: What was the true epoch that established the character of mankind?
We are surely more humane now. Haven't we moved beyond all that?

dawn-019-1.q: Explain how the feeling of custom keeps us from improving our morals.

dawn-020-1.q: Why do people who break the law often come to be admired later?

dawn-021-1.q: What do conscientious people say when following a moral rule leads to misfortune?
I did everything right and it still turned out badly. Was I wrong to follow the rules?

dawn-022-1.q: Isn't faith the essential thing, with good actions following naturally from it?
I've been waiting until I feel confident before I start acting on my ideals. Is that the right order?

dawn-023-1.q: How did superstition make man feel more powerless than necessary?
Describe how fear of a world of living things shaped the history of culture.

dawn-024-1.q: Why is it so hard to test a moral precept the way we test a recipe?
Compare testing a recipe with testing a moral rule.

dawn-026-1.q: What do the rules of polite society share with the animal kingdom?
Explain the resemblance between polite social rules and the camouflage of animals.

dawn-027-1.q: Isn't it dishonest to promise a passion will last forever?

dawn-028-1.q: Why did people take a cheerful state of mind as an argument?
I have a good feeling about a big decision. Should I take that feeling as a reason?

dawn-029-1.q: How did the Greeks act out their virtues?
How did Christianity change the show of virtue into a show of sin?

dawn-031-1.q: Where does man's pride in spirit come from?
Isn't the human mind what separates us from animals?

dawn-032-1.q: Why do we resist the discovery that our moral suffering rests on an error?
Explain why moral suffering feels consoling.

dawn-033-1.q: How did people come to despise real causes and consequences?
Tell me how fear of demons made us despise real causes.

dawn-035-1.q: My friends tell me to trust my feelings and follow my heart. Where do my feelings actually come from?

dawn-036-1.q: Were the first inventors greater than the inventors of today?
Everyone praises the ancients as the true geniuses, and modern discoveries as mere technique. Is that fair?

dawn-037-1.q: Does showing that something is useful explain why it exists?
Explain why showing that something is useful does not tell us why it exists.

dawn-038-1.q: Why did the Greeks think of hope and envy so differently from us?

dawn-039-1.q: What are the consequences of the doctrine of pure spirit?
Tell me what happens to a people that teaches contempt for the body.

dawn-040-1.q: How do meaningless rituals become sacred, and what good comes of them?
Explain how absurd rituals became the training ground of thought.

dawn-041-1.q: Aren't religious and artistic people a blessing to the practical world?
Tell me what harm contemplatives, artists and priests have done to those who act.

dawn-043-1.q: What are the different faculties of a good thinker?
Tell me all the things a thinker must have and how each was once mistaken for the goal.

dawn-044-1.q: Why does knowing the origin of things matter less the more we understand it?
Tell me why the search for origins no longer promises salvation.

dawn-045-1.q: Would humanity ever sacrifice itself for knowledge?
Describe what knowledge might one day demand of humanity.

dawn-046-1.q: Tell me why doubt's pillow made Pascal angry.

dawn-047-1.q: How do words block our path to knowledge?
Explain how words have become fossils that block understanding.

dawn-048-1.q: Is "know thyself" the whole of science?
Say what you mean when you say things are the boundaries of man.

dawn-049-1.q: Doesn't the progress of humanity show human greatness?
Does knowing we come from animals make us smaller or more honest?

dawn-051-1.q: Should we be indulgent towards the great, or towards everyone?
Comment on Mill's plea to be indulgent toward the great one-eyed.

dawn-054-1.q: Does worrying about an illness make it worse?
Tell me why one should soothe a patient's imagination.

dawn-055-1.q: Should I distrust any quick fix or easy path to success?

dawn-056-1.q: Why do we feel disgust for a free spirit who becomes a believer?
A friend of mine used to be a free-thinker and has now become a believer. I find myself unreasonably repelled by this. Why?

dawn-057-1.q: Does our age keep the certainties of Christianity while denying the fear behind them?
Tell me what our age has kept from Christianity and what it has lost.

dawn-058-1.q: What was Christianity's protest against philosophy?
Wasn't philosophy's control of the passions a good thing?

dawn-059-1.q: What was the aim of Christianity concerning moral engagements?
Compare the promises of the shortest way to perfection in Christianity and in philosophy.

dawn-060-1.q: What has Christianity done for the European spirit?
You attack Christianity, yet you praise the finest Catholic priests. Isn't that inconsistent?

dawn-061-1.q: If I've never lived without my beliefs, how can I judge them?
Tell me what someone who believes in Christianity owes to himself before he can judge it.

dawn-062-1.q: Explain how a man comes to treat his own opinion as a revelation.

dawn-063-1.q: What did Pascal think of himself and of mankind?
Tell me what Pascal thought about mankind and why he despised his neighbour.

dawn-064-1.q: Does religion hunt for people at their weakest?
Explain how Christianity looks for the ones who can be driven to despair.

dawn-065-1.q: What is the difference between Brahminism and Christianity?
Compare the paths Brahminism and Christianity offer to a feeling of power.

dawn-066-1.q: Should we trust people who claim to have seen what others cannot?
Tell me why the ages of visions valued madness.

dawn-069-1.q: What is the difference between the Greek and the Christian?
Tell me how the Greek and the Christian differ in envy, friendship and pride.

dawn-070-1.q: Was the Church's power in absorbing every culture a sign of strength or coarseness?
Explain why the Christian Church proved so adaptable.

dawn-073-1.q: The early Christians endured suffering with unshakable belief. Doesn't that prove their faith was true?
Does the virtue of Christians prove the truth of Christianity?

dawn-074-1.q: What might an early Christian have thought about guilt and innocence?
Tell me what an early Christian might have thought about facing a powerful judge.

dawn-076-1.q: What did Christianity do to the passions, and to Eros in particular?
Explain what happens to a natural passion when it is regarded with an evil eye.

dawn-077-1.q: We recoil from physical cruelty but hardly notice psychological cruelty. Why?
Tell me how Christianity spread torments of the soul on an unheard-of scale.

dawn-077-2.q: What did the Christian of the Middle Ages fear?
Describe the terrors that haunted a medieval Christian.

dawn-077-3.q: How did Christianity change the death-bed?
Tell me what Christianity did to the way people die.

dawn-078-1.q: How did Christianity link misfortune to guilt?
Terrible things happen to good people and I keep wondering what they did wrong. Where does this thought come from?

dawn-079-1.q: If the self is hateful, as Pascal says, how can anyone love it?
Explain the argument that the Christian idea of the hateful self makes being loved impossible.

dawn-080-1.q: What is the other side of Christian compassion?
Tell me what Christian pity conceals about the neighbour's joy.

dawn-081-1.q: What did the saint say about sin?
Retell the saint's reply to believers who hated sin.

dawn-082-1.q: Do we have to form an opinion on everything?
Tell me your reply to Luther's threat that your life is at stake in what you believe.

dawn-083-1.q: If a chemical imbalance can make us miserable, why do we blame ourselves or the devil?
Explain why we ascribe bodily misery to sin and the devil.

dawn-084-1.q: Why does Christianity fail to cultivate honesty?
Tell me how learned Christians treat the Bible, and what that says about their honesty.

dawn-085-1.q: Why should we not laugh at Greek mythology?
Tell me what deserves admiration in Greek mythology.

dawn-086-1.q: How does the Christian interpret the body?
Explain how Pascal reads every bodily symptom as a sign of salvation or damnation.

dawn-087-1.q: What is the "moral miracle" in Christianity?
Is sudden conversion a genuine transformation or a psychological episode?

dawn-088-1.q: How did Luther put an end to the saintly life of contemplation?
Tell me why you say Luther did more good than harm.

dawn-089-1.q: Why does Christianity call doubt a sin?

dawn-090-1.q: I can't imagine life without meaning. Does that prove that meaning exists?
Explain the argument that life would be intolerable without God and why it fails.

dawn-091-1.q: Could an omniscient God be good if his intentions are so unclear?
Explain why an omnipotent and omniscient God who leaves his purposes unclear might be cruel.

dawn-091-2.q: Tell me what you make of Pascal's hidden God.

dawn-092-1.q: What is left of Christianity for the modern middle class?
Describe what remains of Christianity in the modern middle class.

dawn-093-1.q: What if God were not truth?
Tell me what is wrong with the argument that science cannot be true because it denies God.

dawn-094-1.q: What did Christians sacrifice for their sins?
Tell me why Christians always seem to need a victim.

dawn-095-1.q: Why is the historical refutation of God decisive?
Explain why tracing the origin of belief in God refutes it better than any argument against God.

dawn-096-1.q: What would happen if the millions of non-believers in Europe recognized each other?
Tell me what India's ancient Brahmins understood that Europe has not.

dawn-098-1.q: Are all moral innovations first seen as crimes?
Tell me where new moral judgments come from.

dawn-099-1.q: Why do I keep feeling guilty about things I no longer believe are wrong?
Explain why we keep drawing conclusions from doctrines we no longer believe.

dawn-100-1.q: Will the belief in the moral meaning of existence fade the way the music of the spheres did?
Say what will happen to the belief in a moral meaning of existence.

dawn-101-1.q: Is accepting a belief simply because it is customary a moral failing?
Tell me what it means to accept a belief only because it is customary.

dawn-102-1.q: Isn't it natural to call harmful people evil and helpful people good?
Where do our oldest moral judgments come from?

dawn-103-1.q: If you deny morality, what stops people from doing whatever they like?
Explain exactly in what sense you deny morality.

dawn-104-1.q: Why do we adopt other people's valuations as our own?
I realize most of my values were handed to me. How can I tell which ones are really mine?

dawn-105-1.q: Explain what you mean by pseudo-egoism.

dawn-106-1.q: What is wrong with defining morality as the preservation and advancement of humanity?
Has moral progress made us happier or more discontented?

dawn-107-1.q: Why does morality forbid us to ask "how" and "why"?
Explain why morality forbids us to ask how and why we must act.

dawn-108-1.q: Is there a universal goal of humanity that could ground moral law?
Tell me why moral precepts do not make individuals happy.

dawn-109-1.q: What are the ways of fighting the vehemence of an impulse?
Lay out the six methods of fighting the vehemence of an impulse.

dawn-109-2.q: Can I control a desire by linking it with a painful thought?
Tell me how a painful association can tame a craving.

dawn-109-3.q: When I fight an impulse, is it really me against a craving or one craving against another?
Explain why the will to fight a craving is itself just another craving.

dawn-110-1.q: How does a new craving come to look like a moral aim?
Explain how a new desire disguises itself as a moral goal.

dawn-112-1.q: What is the natural history of duty?
Tell me how duties arise from what others have done for us.

dawn-112-2.q: Are rights just the degree of power others are willing to guarantee?

dawn-112-3.q: Why is it so difficult to be just?
I want to be fair in a dispute where the balance of power keeps changing. What does justice require of me?

dawn-113-1.q: When I want to impress someone, am I really trying to dominate them?
Tell me what the desire for distinction really seeks in other people.

dawn-114-1.q: What can the suffering man teach us about knowledge?
Describe what a man who has suffered long can see that a healthy man cannot.

dawn-114-2.q: How does a suffering man's pride help him endure?
Tell me how pride helps the sufferer endure.

dawn-115-1.q: Do the words we have for our feelings hide the subtle states that make up our character?
Explain why our words for feelings mislead us about our own character.

dawn-116-1.q: What is the oldest of illusions about human action?
I know what I want and why I act. How can you say I don't?

dawn-117-1.q: How are we imprisoned by our senses?
Tell me how our senses imprison us.

dawn-118-1.q: Do I know the people in my life, or only the effect they have on me?
Tell me what we can really know about the people around us.

dawn-119-1.q: How well do we know our own instincts?
Explain why my character depends on which instincts chance happens to feed.

dawn-119-2.q: How do our instincts search for satisfaction through the day?
Tell me how a starved instinct uses my dreams.

dawn-120-1.q: I don't know what I'm doing or what I should do. Is that so bad?
Comfort a sceptic who says he doesn't know what he is doing.

dawn-121-1.q: Do we ever understand cause and effect?
Explain why cause and effect is only a picture of sequence.

dawn-122-1.q: Did the eye develop for the purpose of seeing?
Tell me what the history of the eye shows about purposes in nature.

dawn-123-1.q: How did reason come into the world?
Tell me how reason came into the world.

dawn-124-1.q: When I say "I want," am I like the man who says "I wish the sun to rise"?

dawn-125-1.q: Can I really understand something I cannot do?
Explain why thought feels free while action does not.

dawn-127-1.q: Which human actions are least understood?
Tell me which of our actions we understand least and why.

dawn-128-1.q: If I'm not responsible for my dreams, why do I feel ashamed of them?
Are we responsible for our dreams?

dawn-129-1.q: How do I actually make a decision, given how little I know about my motives?
Explain what really happens when we think we are weighing motives.

dawn-130-1.q: Why do we feel awe and even fondness for chance when it wrecks our plans?
Tell me about the giants of chance who tear our webs of purpose.

dawn-130-2.q: What was Moira for the Greeks?
Explain how the Greeks, Indians and Christians dealt with the realm of chance.

dawn-130-3.q: Is there really a domain of aims and reason apart from chance?
Explain why even our aims and reason are giants that rule us.

dawn-131-1.q: Would the Stoics call today's selfless morality immoral?
Tell me how the ancients differed from us on living for others.

dawn-132-1.q: What is the last echo of Christianity in our morals?
Explain why you call the morality of pity the last echo of Christianity.

dawn-133-1.q: Is compassion really selfless, or is it a kind of self-defence?
A mother running to her injured child has no thoughts of herself. Isn't that pure pity?

dawn-133-3.q: What distinguishes men without pity from compassionate men?
Tell me what separates the compassionate from those who feel no pity.

dawn-134-1.q: Why must we beware of pity?
Would a world in which everyone acted out of pity be a better one?

dawn-136-1.q: Does pity give us a feeling of superiority?
Tell me how pity helps those who see life as misery.

dawn-137-1.q: Why is it a mistake to adopt other people's experiences as our own?
Explain why treating another's suffering as one's own is a double folly.

dawn-138-1.q: How do our feelings change when we see someone we admire suffer?
Tell me why seeing someone we admire suffer makes us tender.

dawn-139-1.q: Is the morality of pity higher than Stoicism?
Surely pity is morally higher than Stoic detachment.

dawn-140-1.q: When a project fails, why do people rush to find someone to blame?
Explain what really happens when a group looks for someone to blame or praise after a war.

dawn-141-1.q: Tell me why dramatic moral outbursts are only a semi-savage stage of morality.

dawn-142-3.q: Where does sympathy for the feelings of others come from?
Explain how fear taught mankind to understand the feelings of others and of nature.

dawn-142-4.q: Schopenhauer said pity blends two people into one. What's wrong with that?
Tell me what you make of the mystic theory that pity fuses two persons into one.

dawn-143-1.q: Can too much care for others become a burden to them?
Imagine what life would be like if the impulse to devote ourselves to others were twice as strong.

dawn-144-1.q: Why should we close our ears to the complaints of others?
Tell me why we should sometimes turn a deaf ear to other people's complaints.

dawn-147-1.q: What would a world of universal benevolence be like?
Explain why people praise love so extravagantly.

dawn-148-1.q: What happens when men no longer believe themselves evil?
Are there any truly moral actions?

dawn-151-1.q: Should lovers be allowed to make vows for life?
Tell me why marriage ought to be a much more serious matter than it is.

dawn-152-1.q: What oath would you recommend in place of the judicial oath?
Tell me what a better judicial oath would be.

dawn-154-1.q: How did the Greeks seek security, and how do we?
Compare how the Greeks and we look for security in thought.

dawn-155-1.q: Why are hazardous enterprises rarer in modern times?
Explain why daring enterprises have become rarer in modern times.

dawn-156-1.q: What did the Greeks fear about being too happy?
Tell me what the Greeks feared about happiness.

dawn-157-1.q: Why does our culture approve of tears and complaints when the ancients despised them?
Explain why ancient philosophers despised tears and complaints that our culture honours.

dawn-158-1.q: Tell me where the modern flatterers are found.

dawn-159-1.q: Why do vain men value the revival of the past?
Explain how vanity feeds the fashion for reviving the past.

dawn-160-1.q: What should the vain, greedy and unwise practice?
Give a prescription for someone whose desires outrun his understanding and whose vanity outruns his desires.

dawn-161-1.q: How should artists represent beauty in our age?
Tell me how art should portray the beauty of our age.

dawn-162-1.q: Why do Europeans treat important things with irony?
Tell me why irony is our habitual response to serious matters.

dawn-163-1.q: What is your reply to Rousseau?
Rousseau thought civilization corrupted natural goodness. Isn't he right?

dawn-165-1.q: Why does a nation not find its most emphasised moral commandments tiresome?
Explain why a people finds tiresome only the virtues it does not need.

dawn-166-1.q: What is shameful about being a wheel in a system of connections?
At my company, advancement depends on who you know and on being a useful wheel. Why does that seem shameful to you?

dawn-167-1.q: Why is unconditional homage to great men a difficulty?
Tell me how Germany's great men made life hard for their admirers.

dawn-167-2.q: Can we take only the good parts of a great man's work and forget the rest?
Tell me what can be done about admiring only part of a great man.

dawn-168-1.q: Why do you esteem Thucydides more than Plato?
Tell me what you admire in Thucydides and how he differs from Plato.

dawn-169-1.q: Why is the Greek genius foreign to us?
Tell me how the Greeks and we differ in what we find sublime.

dawn-172-1.q: Why do warlike men enjoy tragedy?
Explain why tragedy suited the Athenians of Aeschylus's time and not us.

dawn-173-1.q: Does our culture praise hard work because it keeps people from thinking for themselves?
What is the secret behind glorifying work?

dawn-174-1.q: Isn't making life safer and gentler a good goal?
Is our moral fashion driven by fear of danger and desire for security?

dawn-175-1.q: Are we valuing everything, even art and ideas, by supply and demand?
Describe the culture of a society in which commerce is the soul.

dawn-176-1.q: Why can we endure the truth about the recent past?
Tell me why each generation likes criticising its ancestors.

dawn-177-1.q: What should ambitious young men learn about solitude?
Advise ambitious young people caught up in the daily news.

dawn-179-1.q: Why should the most talented minds stay out of politics and economics?
Tell me why the state should take as little of our best minds as possible.

dawn-181-1.q: Tell me why people want to govern.

dawn-182-1.q: What is rough and ready consistency?
Tell me why crude consistency is taken for character.

dawn-183-1.q: What is the morality of a generation brought up under parliamentary rule?
Compare the old moral obedience to the crown with the new obedience to the party.

dawn-184-1.q: What would intractable men do if they made the laws?
Explain how the state's own discipline breeds those who rebel.

dawn-186-1.q: What is wrong with being bound to one's business?
I'm proud of my business and my family expects to carry it on for generations. Is there a downside?

dawn-187-1.q: What would a criminal of a possible future look like?
Describe a future society in which criminals set their own punishment.

dawn-188-1.q: Why do nations prefer intoxication to nourishment?
Tell me why crowds prefer intoxication to food.

dawn-189-1.q: Explain what really drives high politics.

dawn-190-1.q: What was former German culture, and why was it overrated?
Tell me what happened to German culture and why it fooled Europe.

dawn-190-2.q: Why were foreigners fooled by German culture?
Explain the "starlight halo" around German culture.

dawn-194-1.q: Why have teachers of morals had so little success?
Explain why moral teachers have failed and what might work.

dawn-195-1.q: What is wrong with classical education?
Describe what you think was wasted in your classical education.

dawn-197-1.q: Why were the Germans hostile to the Enlightenment?
Tell me what the Germans did to the Enlightenment in the first half of the century.

dawn-197-2.q: What was the danger of setting knowledge below feeling?
Explain how the tools of romanticism turned against it.

dawn-199-1.q: In what respect do we excel the Greeks in nobility?
Tell me why the ancient Greeks' idea of honour seems ignoble to us.

dawn-199-2.q: What is the ignoble secret of the good Greek aristocrat?
Tell me how the Greek aristocrat differed from a chivalric one.

dawn-202-2.q: Could we free ourselves from the ideas of sin and punishment?
Tell me what a society without vengeance and punishment would look like.

dawn-203-1.q: What is wrong with the meals that the well-off classes eat?
Tell me what the fashionable banquet really shows.

dawn-206-1.q: Would higher wages for factory workers remove their real misery?
Explain why raising a factory worker's wages cannot remove his real misery.

dawn-207-1.q: What is the German's strength and weakness?
Tell me what a German can do when he stops obeying.

dawn-207-2.q: Why is a German frivolous in politics?
Why do people who are serious in their work show caprice in politics?

dawn-207-4.q: What is the German idea of morality?
Explain what the German idea of morality demands of a man.

dawn-207-5.q: What happens when a German rises above morality and has to command?
Tell me what happens when a German outgrows morality and must learn to command.

dawn-208-1.q: What is the new thing you want?
Tell me in one line what you want that is new.

dawn-209-1.q: Why are free-thinking moralists scrutinized more harshly than pious ones?
Everyone forgives the moral failings of a preacher but hunts for flaws in a freethinker's life. Why?

dawn-210-1.q: Is there anything ridiculous or sublime in itself?
Explain why nothing is funny, beautiful or sublime in itself.

dawn-211-1.q: Would you want to live forever?

dawn-212-1.q: What do we know of ourselves according to our comparisons with animals?
Tell me how men first learn who they are.

dawn-213-1.q: If my life feels wasted, is society or I to blame?
Explain why some people's lives are failures no matter what society does.

dawn-214-1.q: Why should we not be indulgent towards the unjust sufferer?
Tell me what suffering does to a person's judgment.

dawn-215-1.q: Isn't self-sacrifice the noblest thing a person can do?
What is the morality of victims?

dawn-216-1.q: Why do evil people love music?
Tell me why embittered, suspicious people love music so much.

dawn-217-1.q: What do Germans, Italians and French want from the artist?
Tell me what each nation wants from its artists.

dawn-218-1.q: Can a flaw make someone's virtues more attractive?
Tell me how a musician's flaws make us hunger for his virtues.

dawn-219-1.q: Why is self-humiliation before one we have wronged often deceit?
Explain why self-humiliation before someone I've wronged is often a performance for myself.

dawn-220-1.q: Do pomp and ceremony conceal timidity?
Explain what pomp and ceremony conceal.

dawn-221-1.q: Why is the morality of sacrifice semi-civilised?
Tell me what a morality of sacrifice says about a people's stage of civilisation.

dawn-223-1.q: Tell me what every writer fears most.

dawn-225-1.q: Why do we quickly despise a man who talks a great deal?
Explain why fast talkers sink in our esteem.

dawn-226-1.q: Tell me why you avoid a famous man whom you admire.

dawn-228-1.q: I've received praise that felt like a dig. Was it?
Tell me how praise can be a disguised form of revenge.

dawn-229-1.q: What do we know of the exultation of human pride?
Tell me what the pride of a tortured man is like.

dawn-230-1.q: Can utilitarianism be used to both support and refute morality?
Explain why arguing for morality from its utility fails.

gs-299-1.q: What should we learn from artists?

gs-300-1.q: What is the prelude to science?

gs-301-1.q: What is the illusion of the contemplative?

gs-304-1.q: Which kind of moral system do you prefer?

gs-309-1.q: Tell me why the wanderer weeps at his own love of truth.

gs-310-1.q: What is the relation of will and wave?
Describe the will as a wave.

gs-311-1.q: Why is it hard to cause pain to others with my truth?
Tell me why the thinker hesitates to hurt others.

Tell me why you will not paint martyrs.

gs-314-1.q: What are your lion and eagle?
Tell me what you want from your lion and your eagle.

Tell me how you would like your life to end.

Tell me why we mistake a passing phase of life for a permanent one.

gs-320-1.q: What do you want to create?

gs-327-1.q: Why do people think thinking must be gloomy?
Tell me why thinking is not supposed to be joyful.

gs-329-2.q: Has the attitude toward work and leisure changed?

gs-330-1.q: Tell me what a thinker needs in place of applause.

gs-332-1.q: What is the evil hour of the philosopher?
Tell me about the philosopher's evil hour.

gs-333-1.q: Is understanding a compromise among conflicting impulses?
Explain what happens inside us when we "understand" something.

Tell me why great men don't shine visibly like the sun.

gs-337-1.q: What is peculiar about the historical sense?
Describe the historical sense as a virtue and a sickness of our age.

gs-338-1.q: Is it to your advantage to be compassionate?
Why does being helped by someone else sometimes make my suffering shallower?

gs-338-2.q: What is the religion of smug ease?
Tell me what lies behind the religion of compassion.

gs-338-3.q: Why do we take refuge in the religion of pity?
What does compassion allow us to escape?

Tell me what Socrates's last words meant.

gs-341-1.q: Would you want to live your life again infinitely?

What does our cheerfulness signify after God's death?

gs-343-2.q: What does the open sea mean for the discerner?
Describe the open sea that now lies before the discerner.

gs-344-2.q: Where does science get its belief that truth is more important than anything else?

gs-347-1.q: Is the need for belief a measure of weakness?
Tell me why most people still need faith.

gs-349-1.q: Is self-preservation the fundamental instinct of life?
Is the struggle for survival an exception to the will to power?

gs-350-1.q: What is the struggle against the church about?
Tell me what the fight against the church is really a fight between.

gs-351-1.q: Why do people honour priestly natures as wise?
Explain why philosophers and the people disagree about what wisdom is.

gs-351-2.q: Why do philosophers not regard the priest as a sage?
Tell me why the priest is not a sage to philosophers.

gs-353-1.q: What is the real invention of a founder of a religion?
Explain what founders of religions really invent.

Explain why becoming conscious falsifies and generalises our experience.

gs-355-2.q: Why are natural sciences more certain than psychology?
Tell me why natural science is surer than psychology.

How will Europe become more artistic?

Why does the stage-player mentality make Europe unable to build lasting things?

gs-357-5.q: Was Schopenhauer's pessimism a German event?

gs-358-3.q: What is the plebeianism of the spirit?

gs-359-1.q: Who are the most dangerous advocates of morality?

gs-359-2.q: Is the philosopher's pretension to wisdom a means of concealment?
Tell me why some philosophers hide behind wisdom.

gs-361-1.q: What is the problem of the actor?
Tell me what the artist and the actor have in common.

gs-365-1.q: How does the anchorite go among men?
Tell me how the recluse gets along among men.

gs-366-1.q: How do you judge the value of a book?
Do learned books distort the soul of their authors?

gs-367-1.q: What is the distinction between monologic art and art before witnesses?
Tell me the difference between art made alone and art made for an audience.

gs-369-1.q: Can an artist create things he does not like?

gs-371-1.q: Why are we unintelligible ones misunderstood?

gs-373-2.q: Is a scientific interpretation of the world the most meaningful?
Tell me what is wrong with a purely mechanical interpretation of the world.

gs-374-1.q: Are there infinite interpretations of the world?

gs-375-1.q: Why are modern thinkers wary of strong convictions?

gs-380-1.q: How can we look at our own morality from the outside?

gs-381-1.q: Why does a writer not want to be understood by everyone?

gs-382-1.q: Tell me what great healthiness is and why the seeker of many ideals needs it.

gs-382-2.q: What is the ideal of the spirit that plays naively with everything holy?
Describe the ideal of a spirit that plays with everything holy.

gs-383-1.q: What do the spirits of the book demand of the author in the epilogue?
Tell me how the epilogue asks us to read the book.
